paragraphs: R’ Shimon, the scribe of Tarkhanes.

Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 4:5 relates that his townspeople asked him to stop halfway through a verse when reading Torah, so that they could read with their children. He asked R’ Chanina, who answered: “Even if they cut off your head, do not obey them.” They removed him from his position as scribe. He went down to Babylonia, came to R’ Shimon ben Yosina and recounted the incident. R’ Zeira said: “Had that scribe lived in my days, I would have appointed him a sage.”

notes.text: The supplied ניזמי is damaged; the checked text has בימוי, “in my days.” Its place-name is Terbent, distinct from Hyman’s Tarkhanes. The English follows the intelligible parallel while preserving the source question.

No new primary scalar was returned. The earlier recorded Megillah comparison has בימוי, in my days, and Terbent, versus supplied ניזמי and Tarkhanes. That supports a contextual rendering but does not prove a nun/bet or zayin/vav error history. The townspeople wanted to read WITH THEIR CHILDREN, not merely have the children read; that relationship is restored. The half-verse request, refusal even under threat of beheading, dismissal, journey and final conditional appointment remain complete. Zeira is a contextual ר״ז expansion; uninspected abbreviated personal titles remain R’.

Hyman’s print (vol. III, p. 1227) reads ביומוי, “in my days,” as does the consulted Jerusalem Talmud Megillah passage. The supplied transcription reads ניזמי. Hyman says the townspeople wanted to read with their children. The consulted edition’s English has the children reading the sentences and calls the town Terbent. The fuller account also records a discussion about dividing and then recombining the verses and renders Zeira’s proposed appointment as Rabbi.
